chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare India’s two points (9% in 2011, 10.5% in 2024) and note how the gap with the highest-prevalence neighbour narrowed over the same period.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not conclude that 10.5% is low or unalarming just because a neighbour has 13.2%; the absolute adult population affected is enormous.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Look at the upward slope for India and its neighbours; the key takeaway is the rapid rise, not just the current number.

chartExplainers.visualId: The quiet burden: mental illness and joint disease
chartExplainers.title: The quiet burden: mental illness and joint disease
chartExplainers.takeaway: The disability burden from mental and musculoskeletal disorders has more than doubled since 1990, reaching 30.4 million and 26.7 million DALYs in 2023.
chartExplainers.detail: Together these two categories now account for over 57 million years lived with disability, rivaling the toll of many infectious diseases. The near-tripling of mental disorder DALYs (from 11.8 million) reflects better recognition but also genuine increases in depression and anxiety. Musculoskeletal disorders, too, have surged as populations age and sedentary life spreads. Because these conditions rarely kill, they remain under-reported and under-funded; the true burden is likely higher. For an ordinary Indian, this means a growing share of life is spent in pain, immobility, or psychological distress, eroding productivity and family well-being.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: A healthier India must address not just mortality but the years lived with disability that hollow out daily life.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Note that the vertical axis measures DALYs (disability-adjusted life years), which combine time lost to disability or early death, but here almost entirely from disability.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not interpret these as death counts; these are years lived with a health loss, so a rise can signal both worsening health and improved diagnosis.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The steep climb since 1990 for both bars is the main pattern; the numbers are large and growing.

chartExplainers.visualId: India's biggest killers, by risk factor
chartExplainers.title: India's biggest killers, by risk factor
chartExplainers.takeaway: Air pollution remained the top risk factor in 2023, causing 2.01 million deaths, while deaths attributed to high body-mass index surged tenfold from 39,000 in 1990 to nearly 400,000.
chartExplainers.detail: The 2023 ranking reveals a dual challenge: traditional environmental risks like unsafe water have plummeted (from 1.09 million deaths to 0.31 million), but metabolic and modern risks have exploded. High blood pressure now kills 1.57 million, more than doubling since 1990, and high glucose accounts for 0.97 million deaths. The tenfold rise in BMI-attributed deaths signals an obesity epidemic that will only worsen if unchecked. Because individuals can have multiple risk factors, the death numbers overlap and should not be summed. For an average Indian, the shift means that the threats to life are increasingly from what we breathe and how we eat, rather than from infections.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Identifying the leading killers guides where prevention and policy can save the most lives.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Focus on the relative lengths of the 2023 bars, and compare with the 1990 values mentioned in labels to gauge speed of change.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not add up the death tolls from each bar; a single death can be attributed to more than one risk factor, so sums would double-count.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The two largest bars (air pollution and high blood pressure) dominate; the tenfold rise in high BMI deaths is the hidden shock.

chartExplainers.visualId: Air pollution's toll, household and total
chartExplainers.title: Air pollution's toll, household and total
chartExplainers.takeaway: Total air pollution deaths rose sharply from 1.3 million in 1990 to 2.01 million in 2023, entirely because of surging outdoor pollution, as household pollution deaths slightly dipped from 1.04 million to 0.94 million.
chartExplainers.detail: The gap between the total and household lines represents deaths from outdoor (ambient) air pollution, which roughly quadrupled over three decades. Improved access to clean cooking fuels is slowly reducing indoor smoke, but this gain has been overwhelmed by emissions from vehicles, industry, and crop burning. In 2023, outdoor pollution accounted for more than half of all air-pollution-related deaths. The modelled estimates imply that lung and heart diseases from ambient fine particles now affect not just urban but also rural populations. For an ordinary Indian, the air they breathe outside is becoming deadlier even as the kitchen smoke recedes.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It explains why overall air pollution mortality keeps rising despite success against indoor smoke, and highlights the need for different interventions.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare the two lines over time; the widening distance between them shows outdoor pollution’s growing share.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not mistakenly think the household line is separate from the total; household air pollution is a subset, so the difference between the two lines approximates outdoor deaths.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Watch how the upper line (total) rises steeply while the lower line (household) stays flat or slightly falls; that gap is the outdoor pollution story.

chartExplainers.visualId: Who pays for Indian healthcare is changing
chartExplainers.title: Who pays for Indian healthcare is changing
chartExplainers.takeaway: Out-of-pocket spending fell from 64.2% to 43.4% of total health expenditure between 2014 and 2023, while the government share rose to 43.7%.
chartExplainers.detail: The two lines crossed in 2020-21, signalling that government financing now edges ahead of household spending for the first time in the NHP series. But these are shares of a total that remains small: government health spend is still about 1.4% of GDP, so the shift partly reflects stalled out-of-pocket growth rather than a surge in public funding. For an ordinary Indian, the decline means a shrinking portion of each health rupee comes directly from her pocket, yet the absolute burden can still rise if incomes do not keep pace with medical inflation. The rapid change since 2018 coincides with the rollout of state-funded insurance schemes like PMJAY, which channel public money through private providers rather than directly expanding government hospitals. Even with crossing lines, out-of-pocket payments still dominate spending on medicines and outpatient care, where insurance rarely covers the bill.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The out-of-pocket share is the single most important indicator of financial risk in a health system, and its fall suggests improved, though still incomplete, protection.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Watch the two lines since 2013-14: the government share climbs while out-of-pocket drops; they meet at just over 43% each in 2022-23.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read this as a surge in total health spending; government expenditure as a share of GDP has barely budged.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On small screens, focus on the crossing point in 2020-21.

chartExplainers.visualId: What a hospital stay costs, public vs private
chartExplainers.title: What a hospital stay costs, public vs private
chartExplainers.takeaway: A private hospitalisation cost 56,215 rupees on average in 2025, over eight times the 6,937 rupees in a government facility.
chartExplainers.detail: The gap has more than doubled from 2014, when the private-to-public ratio was 4.2; private costs rose 118% while public costs crept up only 13% in current rupees. Since these are nominal figures, part of the rise reflects general inflation, but the wedge between the two sectors widened even after adjusting for price changes. For a rural household, a private episode can consume a year’s income, pushing them toward the public system they increasingly avoid. This divergence is fuelled by private-sector consolidation, high-end capital investments, and weak price regulation, while public hospitals rely on flimsy budget increases. The human meaning is stark: choosing the sector where most Indians now get hospitalised often means facing a bill that can tip a family into poverty.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The cost gap captures the tension between where Indians go for care and what they can afford, a central question for health equity.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Note the scale difference: the public line stays almost flat near the bottom, while the private line shoots upward.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not assume the public cost is clinically comparable; case-mix and quality differ, yet the gap is too wide to be explained only by severity.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The private line’s steep climb may be hidden; scroll to see the full y-axis.

chartExplainers.visualId: Where Indians actually get hospitalised
chartExplainers.title: Where Indians actually get hospitalised
chartExplainers.takeaway: In 2025, 57.9% of rural and 64.6% of urban hospitalisation cases were treated in private facilities, up from around 56% in both sectors in 1996.
chartExplainers.detail: The private sector has long been the majority provider, but the rural share crept upward only recently, crossing the old plateau after 2018. This persistent reliance challenges the narrative that rural Indians default to public hospitals; instead, even in villages, six in ten patients now bypass free or low-cost government beds. The shift coincides with NSS data showing that while government hospitalisation costs remain low, the private cost has spiked, suggesting people are paying more for often the same curative care. It also reflects supply-side realities: the number of private hospital beds per capita has grown faster than public-bed expansion, and schemes like PMJAY funnel public money to empanelled private hospitals rather than strengthening government infrastructure. For a landless labourer, the default is no longer the district hospital but a small-town private nursing home that drains household savings.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Where people get admitted reveals whether the public system is absorbing demand and whether policy subsidies are shaping real choices.
chartExplainers.howToRead: The rural line (once lower) has risen and now hovers just below the urban line; both have drifted up slowly over three decades.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read a rise in private share as a vote of confidence in quality; it can also mean public facilities are overcrowded or absent.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The lines are close together; check the y-axis to see the modest upward slope.

chartExplainers.visualId: The insurance revolution
chartExplainers.title: The insurance revolution
chartExplainers.takeaway: Rural health-scheme coverage tripled from 14.1% to 47.4% between 2018 and 2025, overtaking urban coverage.
chartExplainers.detail: The urban share also jumped, from 19.1% to 44.3%, but the rural climb was steeper, erasing the prior urban advantage. This NSS household self-report measure includes government-funded schemes like PMJAY, state insurance programmes, and private insurance, so the explosion after 2018 is largely driven by the rollout of Ayushman Bharat. However, coverage does not equal utilisation; many enrolled households still pay out-of-pocket when they seek care, either because of unawareness, paperwork hurdles, or empanelled hospital distance. The rural surge is notable because rural residents historically had almost no insurance, facing the full brunt of out-of-pocket hospital costs, as seen in the 56,000-rupee private bill. For a daily-wage earner, a card in her pocket is a guardrail she hopes never collapses, but it may not stop the fall.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Insurance coverage is the frontline defence against health-induced poverty, and rapid expansion signals a structural shift in financing.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Notice the rural line starts below urban but overtakes it sharply after 2018; coverage roughly triples in both sectors.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not confuse NSS population coverage with NFHS household coverage or with actual claims; many covered individuals may not use the benefits.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The 2018-2025 leap is dramatic; swipe to see the full rise from the 14% baseline.

chartExplainers.visualId: How families pay the hospital bill
chartExplainers.title: How families pay the hospital bill
chartExplainers.takeaway: 76.7% of hospitalisation cases in India are funded mainly from household savings, and another 15% are financed by borrowing, according to the latest NSS household self-reports.
chartExplainers.detail: This means that only 0.6% of cases are primarily paid through health insurance, exposing nine in ten families to financial shock from a single illness. Savings depletion is the norm, but borrowing at high interest can push a family into long-term debt. Because the data exclude childbirth, this pattern reflects the financing of illnesses and injuries that are often unexpected. The share paid from help by friends or relatives is a thin 1.5%, underscoring that most families cannot rely on social networks to cushion hospital costs. In contrast to the growing rhetoric of insurance expansion, the ground reality remains a near-total absence of risk-pooling for inpatient care.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It shows the depth of out-of-pocket spending, which is the leading cause of medical impoverishment in India.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each bar is the share of hospitalisation cases where that source was the main mode of finance; the tiny insurance bar is barely visible.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not interpret this as expenditure share; 76.7% of cases, not 76.7% of spending.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The insurance bar is just 0.6%, almost invisible on a phone screen.

chartExplainers.visualId: Why patients skip government hospitals
chartExplainers.title: Why patients skip government hospitals
chartExplainers.takeaway: Nearly 30% of patients who skip government hospitals cite poor quality of care as the reason, while another 13% point to long waiting times, revealing that free care is not enough.
chartExplainers.detail: The single largest specific reason, at 29.7%, is perceived poor quality; combined with the 13% who mention long waits, over two-fifths of bypassing is driven by failure in service delivery rather than cost. Distance from a government facility matters for 4.2% of cases, indicating that physical access remains a barrier for a small but important minority. The sizeable ‘other’ category of 36% likely captures unstated reasons such as lack of cleanliness, staff behaviour, or absence of specific services. Since these are self-reported reasons from NSS microdata, they reflect households’ own judgement, not an external quality assessment. For an ordinary family, this means that even when a free bed is available, the fear of receiving inadequate or disrespectful care pushes them toward paying private providers out of pocket.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It explains why government spending on supply-side health infrastructure hasn’t automatically translated into higher utilisation.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each bar is the percentage of non-government hospitalisation cases where that reason was cited as the main factor; the largest specific reason is ‘poor quality’.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not assume that building more government hospitals without improving quality will reduce private-sector dependence.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The ‘Other’ bar is the tallest; on a small screen, look for the second-highest bar for the top named reason.

chartExplainers.visualId: India's health spending against the world
chartExplainers.title: India's health spending against the world
chartExplainers.takeaway: India’s total health expenditure stands at just 3.3% of GDP in 2023, less than half the world average of 10% and even lower than its own 4.1% in 2000.
chartExplainers.detail: This decline of 0.8 percentage points over two decades happened even as GDP grew rapidly, meaning that health spending did not keep pace with the economy. Among comparable countries, Vietnam spends 4.6% and Sri Lanka 3.7%, both higher than India despite similar or lower income levels. This figure includes out-of-pocket spending by households; the government’s share, at about 1.2% of GDP, is one of the lowest globally. For an ordinary Indian, this translates into heavy reliance on personal funds for healthcare, as seen in the earlier chart. The low public investment limits the scale and quality of free services, leaving millions without financial protection against illness.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It quantifies India’s chronic underinvestment in health, which is a root cause of poor health outcomes and high medical poverty.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare India’s bar with the world average and with neighbours; note the downward arrow from 2000 to 2023.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not confuse this with public spending alone; it includes private spending, yet is still dismally small relative to peers.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: India’s bar is the shortest among major Asian economies; try landscape view to see the world average.

chartExplainers.visualId: Doctors and beds, India vs the world
chartExplainers.title: Doctors and beds, India vs the world
chartExplainers.takeaway: India has only 0.72 physicians per 1,000 people, less than half the world’s 1.86, and its hospital bed density has shrunk from 2.13 to 1.59 per 1,000 since 2000.
chartExplainers.detail: The physician density has remained flat at 0.72 between 2014 and 2020, suggesting production of doctors barely offsets population growth. Meanwhile, the world average of physicians rose from 1.52 to 1.86 in the same period, widening the gap. Hospital beds per 1,000 people actually declined, even as the population grew by over 300 million, implying a net loss of bed capacity or a disproportionate concentration in the private sector. This twin shortage means that when a poor family does seek care, they often face overcrowded wards and overburdened doctors, which reinforces the bypassing of government facilities shown in the previous chart. The figures draw from administrative sources and may undercount informal providers, but the stark divergence from the world average points to a deep systemic deficit.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Because even free or subsidised care cannot be delivered without enough doctors and beds, making this a hard physical limit on health improvements.
chartExplainers.howToRead: For each metric, compare India’s latest value to the world’s latest value; note the downward trend in beds.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not assume these numbers include AYUSH practitioners or informal clinics; the physician count is largely allopathic doctors registered with medical councils.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Two numbers to spot: doctors 0.72, beds 1.59; both are far below the world lines.

chartExplainers.visualId: What childbirth costs, by hospital type
chartExplainers.title: What childbirth costs, by hospital type
chartExplainers.takeaway: In private for-profit hospitals, where 35.2% of deliveries happen, 61.5% are C-sections and the average medical spend is Rs 40,452.
chartExplainers.detail: Public hospitals handle 63.8% of deliveries at an average cost of just Rs 2,359, with a C-section rate of only 19.1%. A delivery in a private for-profit hospital costs 17 times more than one in a public facility. The C-section share in private care triples that in public care, a gap that often reflects financial incentives rather than medical necessity. For an ordinary Indian family, choosing a private hospital can mean a high chance of surgical birth and a bill that may push them into debt. The tiny 1% of deliveries in the mid-tier (likely charitable) hospitals carry an intermediate cost and C-section rate, but they barely relieve the overall pattern.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The sharp cost-and-C-section divergence between public and private settings reveals a segmented maternity-care system where affordability and medically justified delivery are not assured, a mixed signal for India’s health progress.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each bar shows the average medical spend; the C-section share (as a percentage) is noted alongside. The delivery share tells you how common each hospital type is.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Concluding that higher C-sections in private hospitals automatically mean better care. They may instead signal over-medicalisation driven by profit or fear of litigation, not health need.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Swipe or scroll sideways to see all three hospital types; the public-private contrast is the core story.

chartExplainers.visualId: How many public health facilities India has
chartExplainers.title: How many public health facilities India has
chartExplainers.takeaway: There are 161,829 sub-centres but only 767 district hospitals: for every district hospital, 211 sub-centres exist.
chartExplainers.detail: The public infrastructure is heavily bottom-heavy. Sub-centres are the first point of care for millions of rural Indians, yet they are not equipped for deliveries or serious illness. The 31,053 primary health centres form the supposed backbone of clinical care, but many lack full-time doctors. The steep drop from PHCs to 6,064 community health centres and just 767 district hospitals means that for complicated cases, the nearest fully-equipped public facility can be far away. These counts are from administrative records and do not reveal whether a facility is staffed, stocked, or functional.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The shape of the public-facility pyramid determines how close ordinary Indians are to basic and emergency care; weak lower tiers undermine the country’s health gains from disease-control programmes.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read the exact numbers; each bar is a different facility type. The steep decline from sub-centres to PHCs shows how stretched the system is.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Treating every sub-centre as operational; many may exist only on paper or lack a health worker, so the actual front-line reach is narrower.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Tap each bar to see the precise count; focus on the huge gap between sub-centres and the hospital tier.

chartExplainers.visualId: India's health workforce, on paper
chartExplainers.title: India's health workforce, on paper
chartExplainers.takeaway: India’s register lists 1.35 million allopathic doctors, but this cumulative total inflates the real number who are still practising.
chartExplainers.detail: The 1.35 million figure includes retirees, emigrants, and those who left clinical work, so the active doctor-to-population ratio is substantially worse than the raw count suggests. Nurses and midwives number 2.56 million, yielding a nurse-to-doctor ratio of about 2:1, which is low by global norms and hints at a skill-mix problem. The 1.71 million AYUSH practitioners further complicate the picture, as not all deliver evidence-based allopathic care. For a person in need, these paper numbers can mislead: you may live in an area with many registered doctors on paper yet still struggle to find a practising physician when you are sick.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Health-workforce supply is the bedrock of getting healthier; counting registrations instead of active staff paints an overly rosy picture that hides rural and functional shortages.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Note the exact registered numbers, but mentally discount them because they are cumulative and not filtered for active or in-position staff.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Dividing 1.35 million by the population to calculate a doctor-to-population ratio; that gives a falsely optimistic number that masks actual availability.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The bar heights show only cumulative registrations; the missing active-workforce story is the real caveat on a small screen.

chartExplainers.visualId: Doctors cluster in a few states
chartExplainers.title: Doctors cluster in a few states
chartExplainers.takeaway: The top four states alone account for over 6 lakh registered doctors, about 44% of the national total, leaving many other states with fewer than 50,000.
chartExplainers.detail: Maharashtra (2.11 lakh), Karnataka (1.49 lakh), Tamil Nadu (1.34 lakh) and Gujarat (1.06 lakh) together claim 6 lakh of the 13.5 lakh registered MBBS doctors. This concentration is only partly explained by population size; it also reflects where medical colleges and urban jobs are located. Per-capita, states like Bihar or Uttar Pradesh, despite large populations, have far fewer registered doctors, starving rural areas of qualified physicians. For an ordinary Indian in a low-registration state, consulting a doctor may require costly travel or reliance on informal practitioners, and the quality of care suffers. The chart shows absolute counts, but the inequality would look even starker when adjusted for population.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: A country cannot get healthier for everyone if medical expertise clumps in a few pockets; the geographic maldistribution directly translates into unequal health outcomes.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Look at the steep drop after the top four bars. The x-axis reports absolute numbers, so large states naturally have more doctors, but the gap is larger than population shares alone explain.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Assuming that states with high absolute numbers necessarily have a good doctor density. They may simply have bigger populations, and the per-capita picture is often less flattering.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Scroll horizontally to see the full list; the dominance of the top four states is the key message.

chartExplainers.visualId: What a month of GLP-1 costs in India
chartExplainers.title: What a month of GLP-1 costs in India
chartExplainers.takeaway: In 2026, the cheapest GLP-1 generic in India still costs ₹9,988 per month, far above the headline ₹220-per-shot prices some firms have announced.
chartExplainers.detail: This amount is more than double the monthly income of a typical Indian household, placing GLP-1s out of reach for all but the wealthy. While the price has fallen dramatically from branded semaglutide at ₹25,148, it remains vastly more expensive than metformin, which costs under ₹100 a month. The gap between the lowest generic price shown (₹9,988) and the reported ₹880 monthly for some generics shows that availability and retail markups keep real costs high. For ordinary Indians with diabetes, even this 'cheap' option means spending a significant share of income on a chronic therapy. Without deeper price cuts or public subsidies, the metabolic benefits of GLP-1s will bypass the vast majority of the 101 million diabetic Indians.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The cost of GLP-1s directly determines whether India’s massive diabetic population can access a drug class that could curb obesity and cardiovascular disease on a population scale.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Look at the wide gap between the tallest bar (branded semaglutide) and the shortest (generic), then compare even the shortest to metformin’s typical cost of under ₹100.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not assume that ₹220-a-shot generics are widely available; the chart shows that actual retail prices remain much higher.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The key contrast is the nearly ₹10,000/month generic vs the ₹25,000/month branded; on a phone, pinch to see the large drop still left.

chartExplainers.visualId: What kills the most Indians
chartExplainers.title: What kills the most Indians
chartExplainers.takeaway: Cardiovascular disease killed an estimated 3.1 million Indians in 2023, about as many as chronic respiratory disease, cancers and diabetes combined.
chartExplainers.detail: This is the death-count view of India’s disease transition, and it is lopsided. Heart and circulatory disease alone account for roughly 3.1 million deaths a year in the GBD 2023 estimates, while chronic respiratory disease (about 1.25 million), cancers (1.06 million) and diabetes (0.6 million) form a distant second tier. The infectious and newborn causes that dominated India’s deaths a generation ago, diarrhoea, pneumonia, tuberculosis and birth complications, have each fallen below half a million. Counts are not the same as risk: because these are absolute numbers, a growing and ageing population lifts them even when death rates fall. What the bar cannot show is age, and the burden chart weights deaths by how early they strike, which is why childhood causes loom larger there than here.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It names, in plain counts, exactly what Indians are now most likely to die of, the clearest single answer to where the health system must aim.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each bar is one cause’s estimated deaths in 2023, ranked from most to fewest. Compare the top bar with the sum of the next few.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read a small bar as a solved problem. About 330,000 tuberculosis deaths a year is still enormous; it only looks small next to heart disease.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The top bar, cardiovascular, is the whole story; scroll for the long tail.

chartExplainers.visualId: What men and women die of in India
chartExplainers.title: What men and women die of in India
chartExplainers.takeaway: Road accidents cause 5.2% of male deaths but only 1.4% of female deaths, while ill-defined causes account for 15.5% of women’s deaths versus 9.7% of men’s.
chartExplainers.detail: Two different stories sit in these bars. The first is biological and behavioural: men die more from cardiovascular disease (30.8% of male deaths versus 26.2% for women) and far more on the roads, where their share is almost four times higher. The second is about records, not bodies. Fever of unknown origin and ill-defined causes together account for more than a fifth of women’s deaths but well under a sixth of men’s, meaning a woman’s death is markedly more likely to be registered without a real diagnosis. Cancers take a slightly larger share of women’s deaths. These are shares of each sex’s own deaths, so they describe composition, not how many die. The figures, pooled over 2017 to 2019, predate the 2023 GBD counts above and come from India’s own registration system.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The verdict on health is partly about fairness, and a death that goes unrecorded is the starkest sign of who the system reaches last.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read each pair as men versus women for the same cause, as a share of that sex’s deaths. The injury gap and the ill-defined gap are the two to watch.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not treat ill-defined as a cause of death. It is the absence of one; a higher share means worse recording, not a mystery illness.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Compare the two bars in each pair: injuries skew male, unrecorded causes skew female.

chartExplainers.visualId: Most Indian deaths still aren't medically certified
chartExplainers.title: Most Indian deaths still aren't medically certified
chartExplainers.takeaway: Only about 23% of registered deaths had a medically certified cause in 2020, up from 14% in 1995, so roughly four in five still do not.
chartExplainers.detail: This single line is the foundation under every cause-of-death number in this article. Medical certification of cause of death rose steadily from 14.2% of registered deaths in 1995 to 22.5% in 2020, then stalled near a fifth. Because certification is concentrated in urban hospitals, it captures almost nothing about how rural India dies, and registration itself misses many deaths entirely. That gap is why the cause data here comes from the SRS verbal-autopsy survey and the GBD model, not from death certificates. The slow rise is genuine progress in how India sees itself; the low ceiling is why so much still has to be estimated.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: A country cannot manage what it does not measure, and India still cannot directly observe the cause of most of its deaths.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Follow the single line upward from 1995 to 2020; it climbs into the low twenties and then flattens.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read the rise as near-complete coverage. At about a fifth, certification is still the exception, not the rule.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: One line: certified deaths climb from 14% to 23%, then stall.

chartExplainers.visualId: Accidents are flat, but suicides are climbing
chartExplainers.title: Accidents are flat, but suicides are climbing
chartExplainers.takeaway: Suicides rose about a fifth from 2011 to 2021, to 1.64 lakh, driven almost entirely by men, while accidental deaths stayed near 4 lakh.
chartExplainers.detail: Two external causes of death, two different stories. Accidental deaths hovered around 4 lakh a year and dipped to 3.74 lakh in the 2020 lockdown when traffic collapsed. Suicides climbed from about 1.36 lakh in 2011 to 1.64 lakh in 2021, with the steepest rise in the COVID years. Almost all of that increase was male: recorded male suicides went from 87,839 to 118,979 while female suicides barely moved, near 45,000. These are police counts, and suicide is widely under-reported, so the real numbers are higher. What the chart cannot show is rate versus count: a growing population lifts both lines even when individual risk is unchanged.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: As infectious deaths retreat, mental distress and injury are taking a larger share of India’s early deaths, a central part of the worse verdict.
chartExplainers.howToRead: The upper line is accidental deaths, the lower is suicides. Watch the suicide line bend upward after 2019.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read flat accidental deaths as safe roads. Counts stayed level while the population grew, so the per-person rate actually fell, and the 2020 dip was the lockdown, not a safety gain.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Two lines: accidents flat near 4 lakh, suicides rising to 1.64 lakh.

chartExplainers.visualId: Tobacco and alcohol are still a male habit
chartExplainers.title: Tobacco and alcohol are still a male habit
chartExplainers.takeaway: More than a third of Indian men (36.3%) use tobacco and nearly a fifth (18.9%) drink alcohol, against 8.4% and 1.1% of women.
chartExplainers.detail: Tobacco and alcohol are the two largest behavioural risks behind India's cancer and cardiovascular burden, and they are overwhelmingly male. In NFHS-6, men's tobacco use was more than four times women's, and male drinking nearly seventeen times female. Both fell only slightly since NFHS-5 (men's tobacco from 38.0% to 36.3%), so this is a stalled risk, not a retreating one. Because the questions are self-reported, the true figures are likely higher, and women's use in particular is probably understated by stigma. What the bars cannot show is the household reach: the disease, spending and lost income from a man's tobacco or alcohol use land on the whole family.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: These are modifiable risks; their stubbornly high male levels are a large part of why the chronic-disease burden keeps rising.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each bar is the latest NFHS-6 share for one sex. Compare men with women within tobacco, then within alcohol.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read women's low numbers as low risk. Self-reporting and stigma understate female use, and secondhand smoke harms non-users too.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Men's bars tower over women's for both tobacco and alcohol.

chartExplainers.visualId: Private hospitals cut far more often
chartExplainers.title: Private hospitals cut far more often
chartExplainers.takeaway: By NFHS-6, 54.1% of births in private facilities were by caesarean, against 16.9% in public ones, a roughly threefold gap.
chartExplainers.detail: India's overall caesarean rate rose from 21.5% to 27.2% between the two survey rounds, but the facility split is the real signal. Private hospitals now deliver more than half of their births surgically, while public facilities sit near 17%. Some rise is medically genuine, as mothers grow older and first births are handled cautiously, but a threefold facility gap is hard to attribute to need alone, because a caesarean bills for far more than a normal delivery. The World Health Organization holds that a population rate above 10 to 15% is rarely justified on medical grounds. What the lines cannot show is harm to mothers and babies from unnecessary surgery, or the out-of-pocket cost it adds.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It is the clearest evidence that India's shift to private care brings more procedures, not just more access, a cost-and-incentive problem at the heart of the health bill.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Two lines across the two survey rounds. The gap between private and public, not the slope, is the point.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read a high caesarean rate as better care. Above the WHO band, more surgery signals incentives or convenience, not safer birth.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Private line sits far above public; both rounds shown.

caveats: World Bank HNP indicators are modelled/harmonised and may not match national survey estimates exactly.
NFHS-5 (2015-16) and NFHS-6 (2019-21) are household surveys with sampling error; NFHS-6 did not include anaemia testing, so anaemia trends cannot be directly compared.
IHME GBD 2023 estimates use statistical models to fill data gaps; they show patterns, not direct measurements.
National Health Accounts (2019) aggregates financial flows but may undercount private spending.
NSS 80th-round (2025) unit data tabulated by Indica provides household-level cost and care utilisation; official MoSPI report may differ.
National Health Profile 2023 (CBHI) registration counts are cumulative and 'on paper', not necessarily active or in-position staff; facility counts carry reporting lag.
NFHS 'persons covered' and NSS 'households covered' are different units of analysis and not directly comparable.
All data reveal associations, not causal relationships.
The GLP-1/Ozempic coda is speculative and based on scenario modelling, not measured outcomes.

The sex-split causes of death are registration shares pooled over 2017-2019, not counts and not the latest year; a large ill-defined or fever-of-unknown-origin share reflects deaths whose cause was never established, more often for women, rather than a real disease.

Accidental-death and suicide figures are police-reported counts (NCRB), widely held to undercount suicide; they are counts not rates, so population growth lifts them, and the 2020 dip in accidents reflects the COVID lockdown.
Tobacco and alcohol use are self-reported in NFHS and almost certainly undercounted, especially among women; the caesarean figures are survey shares for two rounds, not a continuous series.

plannedCharts.title: Indians live much longer than they used to
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The headline answer is survival: India has climbed close to the world line, but not to the best Asian comparators.

plannedCharts.title: Living longer, but not always in good health
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The extra years are not all healthy years; the gap is time lived in illness.

plannedCharts.title: The biggest win is children surviving
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Falling child deaths explain much of the life-expectancy gain.

plannedCharts.title: Maternal mortality fell, but the frontier is much lower
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The path matters more than the rank: India fell sharply, while Sri Lanka and China show how much lower the frontier is.

plannedCharts.title: The old killers are in retreat
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The diseases of being poor and crowded are falling fast in disease-burden terms.

plannedCharts.title: Vaccination went from near-zero to near-universal
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The child-survival gains are backed by a long vaccine build-out.

plannedCharts.title: Care around birth is deepening
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: NFHS shows the service-delivery story directly, including the less comfortable rise in C-sections.

plannedCharts.title: India is training far more doctors than it used to
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Capacity to produce doctors has expanded fast, a genuine investment in the future.

plannedCharts.title: Nutrition improved slowly, and India still looks weak
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The counterweight to the survival story is the slow grind of nutrition.

plannedCharts.title: NFHS says stunting fell, but wasting barely moved
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The India-native survey update: the good news is real, but thin.

plannedCharts.title: NFHS moved in many directions at once
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The honest India-native summary: the newest survey does not move in one direction.

plannedCharts.title: Overweight women, state by state
plannedCharts.subtitle: NFHS-6 (2023-24) · overweight/obese women 15-49, by state · child stunting and thinness carried alongside
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The double burden mapped: states where adult overweight and child undernutrition coexist.

plannedCharts.title: Children thinner, adults heavier
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Undernutrition is falling while adult overweight rises: two malnutritions at once.

plannedCharts.title: The poorest child still starts far behind
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank HNP by wealth quintile · latest India survey year available
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The average hides the fairness problem: wealth still changes nutrition, access and survival.

plannedCharts.title: One India average hides many health transitions
plannedCharts.subtitle: NFHS-6 · highest state or UT minus lowest state or UT
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The same indicator can describe very different state realities.

plannedCharts.title: Rural and urban India have different health problems
plannedCharts.subtitle: NFHS-6 · absolute rural-urban gap in India values
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Rural-urban gaps are not a simple backward-forward story.

plannedCharts.title: What India dies of has flipped
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The single biggest shift in Indian health: lifestyle disease overtook infection.

plannedCharts.title: India's NCD share, against its neighbours
plannedCharts.subtitle: IHME GBD 2023 · non-communicable share of disease burden · selected countries
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Richer and older countries flipped earlier; India flipped while still poor.

plannedCharts.title: The diseases that carry India's burden, 1990 vs now
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The leaderboard of disease burden reshuffled: heart disease up, childhood infection down.

plannedCharts.title: Adults are getting heavier and more diabetic
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Measured, not modelled: the household survey caught metabolic risk rising between rounds.

plannedCharts.title: Diabetes across the neighbourhood
plannedCharts.subtitle: IHME GBD 2023 · diabetes prevalence · selected countries
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: India's diabetes burden in cross-country context.

plannedCharts.title: The quiet burden: minds and joints
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Conditions that rarely kill but increasingly disable, and are easy to overlook.

plannedCharts.title: India's biggest killers, by risk factor
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Deaths sorted by the risk factor behind them, India 2023.

plannedCharts.title: Air pollution's toll, household and total
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The single largest environmental risk, and how much is indoor smoke.

plannedCharts.title: Who pays for Indian healthcare is changing
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The most important number in Indian health financing: the out-of-pocket share is finally falling.

plannedCharts.title: What a hospital stay costs, public vs private
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The price gap between a public and a private bed, across NSS rounds.

plannedCharts.title: Where Indians actually get hospitalised
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The private sector now handles most hospitalisations, even in villages.

plannedCharts.title: The insurance revolution
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Health-scheme coverage roughly tripled, and PMJAY flipped the rural-urban gradient.

plannedCharts.title: How families pay the hospital bill
plannedCharts.subtitle: NSS 80th round (2025) · Indica tabulation of unit data · major source of finance
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Most stays are paid from savings, but a sizeable share is financed by borrowing.

plannedCharts.title: Why patients skip government hospitals
plannedCharts.subtitle: NSS 80th round (2025) · Indica tabulation of unit data · reasons for not using a government facility
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Free care exists; people still pay private. This is why.

plannedCharts.title: India's health spending against the world
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: India spends a strikingly small share of GDP on health.

plannedCharts.title: Doctors and beds, India vs the world
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: India has fewer doctors and hospital beds per person than the world average.

plannedCharts.title: What childbirth costs, by hospital type
plannedCharts.subtitle: NSS 80th round (2025) · Indica tabulation of unit data · average medical spend per delivery; C-section share carried alongside
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The cost and the C-section rate both jump in private hospitals.

plannedCharts.title: India's public health system, in counts
plannedCharts.subtitle: NHP 2023 (CBHI) · Rural Health Statistics, as on 31 March 2023
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: India's own count of the public scaffolding, from village sub-centre to district hospital.

plannedCharts.title: India's health workforce, on paper
plannedCharts.subtitle: NHP 2023 (CBHI) · cumulative registrations with professional councils
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The official headcount of doctors, nurses and others, with a heavy caveat.

plannedCharts.title: Doctors cluster in a few states
plannedCharts.subtitle: NHP 2023 (CBHI) · MBBS doctors registered with state councils, upto 31.12.2022
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Even on paper, registered doctors are concentrated in a handful of states.

plannedCharts.title: What a month of GLP-1 costs in India
plannedCharts.subtitle: Press-verified retail prices, mid-2026 · representative monthly cost, ranges in the data
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Deliberately speculative: after the March 2026 patent cliff, GLP-1 prices fell off a wall, and the effect on India's metabolic burden could be large but is genuinely unknown.

selectionRules: Start from the page question, not from the indicator name.
Choose the smallest set of visuals that explains scale, trend, structure, comparison, and caveat.
Prefer mobile-friendly charts: line charts with sparse ticks, horizontal bars, share strips, pyramids only when essential, and no dense tables.
Use one strong pull quote only when the evidence supports it with a number.
Add glossary blocks for technical terms that normal readers may not know.
caveats: Use only figures present in lockedNumbers or sourceSummaries.
If a related theme indicator is present, you may use it for context, but do not pretend it is the main answer.
If source coverage is thin, say so directly.
Do not compare states, districts, or cities unless the evidence packet contains those geographies.
forbiddenClaims: Do not infer causality from a trend unless the evidence explicitly supports it.
Do not cite a source that is not present in sourceSummaries.
